Ricardo is 21, works as no occupation, alone.

How life is going overall. poor.

What brings them here now. Ricardo reports feeling unable to manage the pressures currently on him — a freelance album-cover commission he has not opened in weeks, part-time shifts at the grocery, and a community-college enrolment deadline — since his two-year marriage ended four months ago. Alongside this he describes ongoing distress connected to a car accident last year, which he was driving for and in which his wife was hurt: he has not driven at night since, detours around the highway out toward the coast, and still hears the sound of the crash when he lies down to sleep. The strain shows most in his close relationships — the two friends he used to cook for left unanswered, his mother's calls dodged, the family tamalada skipped — though he tells everyone who asks that he is fine; he denies drinking or using anything to cope, and denies any thoughts of harming himself.
What they want out of support: I want to be able to answer my mom and my friends without my chest going tight, and finish a commission without the whole week falling apart around it.

Predisposing. Ricardo grew up in a full, loud household where his mother's love came free but his father's warmth had to be earned — unload the truck, work the pit, and there were stories and a hand on the back of his neck at dinner; spend the Saturday hunched over alebrijes at the kitchen table and the room went quiet around him. His father carried the family the only way he knew how, with his back and his hours, so a son who drew all day looked to him like a son who would need carrying. When Ricardo dropped out at seventeen, the two of them barely spoke for the better part of a year, and even after they made peace he never showed his father a sketchbook again.

Precipitating. Four months ago his wife Marisol moved out of the apartment they had shared since he was nineteen and back to her mother's place in Liberty — the quiet end of a marriage that had been buckling since the accident he was driving for last year, when she was hurt and he went months barely able to talk to her about any of it. He kept the job and the apartment, but the life around them thinned fast: Sunday dinners stopped, the group chat with the two friends he used to cook for went quiet from his side, and the album-cover commission he had been proud of has sat unopened since October. Three weeks ago Marisol came for the last of her boxes, and it was that weekend — the half-emptied closet, her mug still in the cupboard — that set him looking for somewhere to actually say any of this.

Perpetuating. It is one strategy in three shapes: keep the difficulty where nobody can see it, and take the cost out at night. It has protected everyone from him, as he would put it, while quietly removing the dinners, the friends and the work that used to make a week stand up.
- hiding_needs: Everyone gets 'estoy bien, nomás ocupado' — he told his mother the separation was mutual and calm when it wasn't, and told his closest friend that a deadline kept him from dinner; when his mother pushes past the stock answer he goes short with her and ends the call. - avoidance: He opens the client's messages about the album cover, reads them, and closes them again, telling himself he will reply once the work looks like something; he takes the farm roads into town so as not to touch the stretch of highway where the car went over, and the coastal marshes he used to photograph have been off the table since.

she said she'd stop calling
That's a heavy thing to hear from her. How did that land for you when she said it?
like she was the one getting hung up on. i said one thing about it being a bad time and thats it, now im the bad guy
So you set a boundary and somehow ended up cast as the one in the wrong. That's a frustrating spot to be in. What was going on for you when you said it was a bad time?
i was at work. she called twice and i cant be on the phone in the middle of a shift
That's completely reasonable — you can't take a call mid-shift. Did she know you were at work when she called?
yeah she knows my shifts. shes called me at work a hundred times
So this isn't a one-off — she knows your shifts and calls anyway. What do you make of that?
i dunno, shes my mom, thats just how she is
"That's just how she is" sounds like something you've had to tell yourself a lot. Does it feel okay to you, or more like something you've gotten used to?
i dont think theres some hidden thing there. shes my mom, she calls, thats it
Fair enough — I'll take you at your word there. So the call itself isn't the issue; it's more the hanging up and the "I'll stop calling" that stuck with you?
yeah. i was gonna call her back later that night and then she did that
So you had every intention of calling her back, and she closed the door before you got the chance. What's it like sitting with that?
its not just her. beto texted me about a tamalada saturday and i havent even opened it

cause if i go theyre gonna ask stuff. and id have to sit there and answer it
Being asked stuff — that's the part you'd rather skip. What kind of questions are you expecting?
like wheres mari. how am i holding up. how come i never come around anymore
Those are a lot of questions to sit through. Who's Mari to you?
mari. marisol. she was my wife. she moved out four months ago
Four months — that's still pretty fresh. Does Beto know about Marisol moving out?
he knows we split up. he doesnt know the rest of it
So he knows about the split, but there's more that he doesn't know. What's the part you've kept to yourself?
i dont really wanna get into all that right now

the tamalada thing. i could just text him back something short and not go

if i say ill come and then i dont, thats worse than not answering

saying nothing is easier. but ive already done that with the band thing and that just turned into nothing too

maybe just opening it tonight and sending back something dumb. like a "lol what time"

cause its not me saying im good or making up some excuse. its just a question back

then he tells me a time and suddenly its saturday and im walking into a room full of people who all know

probably that they feel sorry for me. like im the guy whose wife left

the look. i dont want anyone looking at me like that

yeah. in a second. i used to be the one cooking for those guys

yeah. i miss it. thats the stupid part
